CH is like English “ch”: chaqueta = “cha-ke-ta”. QUE in the same word is read “ke”.
Some words lose their written accent in the plural because the number of syllables changes: pantalón → pantalones, jamón → jamones. The stressed syllable stays the same: pan-ta-LÓN, pan-ta-LO-nes.
Review c + e/i (“th” in Spain): cien, ciento, precio, cincuenta.
1. This, that, that over there: este / ese / aquel
English has two degrees (this / that). Spanish has three, depending on how far away the thing is:
This jacket (the one I’m holding) is black.
And that blue one (next to you)?
That coat (over there) is very expensive.
In everyday speech “este” and “ese” are the most common. “Aquel” appears when you really point at something far away.
Don’t confuse “esta” (this) with “está” (is, the verb ESTAR). The accent makes the difference!
“Cien” is exactly 100. From 101 to 199 you use “ciento”: ciento veinte (120), ciento cincuenta y cinco (155).
The hundreds agree with feminine nouns: doscientos euros, but doscientas personas. And “mil” has no “un”: 1000 = mil (not “un mil”).
The irregular ones: quinientos (500, not “cincocientos”), setecientos (700), novecientos (900).
Between hundreds and tens there is NO “y” (unlike English “and”): 125 = ciento veinticinco. “Y” only appears between tens and units: 135 = ciento treinta y cinco.
Esa es más barata que esta.
El azul es menos caro que el negro.
Es tan bonita como la otra.
Don’t say “más bueno”. Correct: “Esta tienda es mejor que esa”.
PODER changes o to ue, following the “boot” rule from chapter 8. It is followed directly by the infinitive, without “to”.

Me lo llevo. / Me la llevo.
“Lo” for masculine things (el abrigo → me lo llevo), “la” for feminine ones (la chaqueta → me la llevo).
The hundreds agree with the feminine.

In Spain the big sales start in January. Lucía describes a shopping day with her friend.
In Spain the winter sales start on the seventh of January.
On that day the shops in the centre are full of people.
My friend Inés and I go shopping on Calle Preciados.
Inés wants a long coat. I need some shoes and some trousers.
In the first shop, Inés sees a gorgeous grey coat, but it costs three hundred euros.
“It’s really expensive!”, says Inés. “With the discount it’s a hundred and eighty,” answers the shop assistant.
Inés tries on the coat. It’s a little big on her, but there’s a smaller size.
In the end she takes it. She’s very pleased.
I find some black trousers for twenty euros: they’re cheaper than in other shops.
The shoes are harder to find. Some are pretty but uncomfortable; others are comfortable but ugly.
After three hours we’re tired and hungry.
We have a hot chocolate with churros in a café. It’s the best part of the day!
Tomorrow I’m going again: I still don’t have any shoes.
“le queda grande” = it’s too big on her
On Monday Tom has a very important job interview at a company in Madrid.
His problem: he has no smart clothes. His wardrobe has only T-shirts, jeans and trainers.
On Saturday he goes shopping with Lena to a big shop on Gran Vía.
First he looks for a jacket. The shop assistant shows him a black one and a grey one.
The black one costs two hundred euros. The grey one costs a hundred and twenty. Tom chooses the grey one: it’s cheaper and it suits him better.
Then he needs a shirt. Lena says: “This blue one is gorgeous.” But Tom prefers the white one.
“The white one is more classic,” he explains. He tries on both. In the end he buys the blue one: Lena is right.
For his feet, he buys some brown shoes. They’re a little uncomfortable, but very smart.
In total he pays three hundred and forty euros. That’s a lot of money for Tom!
On Monday Tom arrives at the interview in his new clothes. He looks very good and he’s a little nervous.
The interviewer is very nice… and she’s wearing a blue shirt, just like Tom’s.
They both laugh. “We have the same taste,” she says. It’s a good start.
A week later, Tom got an email: the job was his.
“le queda mejor” = it suits him better
